primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Estrogen deficiency increases osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, producing loss of trabecular and cortical bone mass while mineralization remains normal.
vignette: A 66-year-old postmenopausal woman has a low-trauma vertebral compression fracture. Serum calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase are normal.
lead: Which cellular change most directly contributes to this disorder?
distractor_notes: Defective mineralization causes osteomalacia, which often alters mineral metabolism.
Primary collagen synthesis defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta rather than age-related osteoporosis.
Absence of PTH does not explain common postmenopausal bone loss.
Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, not classic osteoporosis.
key_expl: Postmenopausal estrogen loss increases osteoclast activity and bone resorption, causing osteoporosis with normal mineralization.
objective: Explain postmenopausal osteoporosis through increased bone resorption.
clues: normal mineral labs in a postmenopausal woman

sources.title: Osteoporosis
sources.support: NIAMS describes osteoporosis as loss of bone mass and strength, especially after menopause.

sources.title: Osteoporosis
sources.support: MedlinePlus identifies menopause and bone loss as major osteoporosis risk factors.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Vitamin D deficiency reduces intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, impairing mineralization of growing bone and widening growth plates.
vignette: A 2-year-old child with little sun exposure has bowed legs, delayed growth, and widening of the wrists. Serum alkaline phosphatase is elevated.
correct: Rickets due to vitamin D deficiency
distractor_notes: Osteogenesis imperfecta causes fractures and blue sclerae rather than growth-plate widening from poor mineralization.
Achondroplasia causes disproportionate short stature from FGFR3 signaling, not bowing due to mineral deficiency.
Scurvy causes defective collagen hydroxylation and bleeding, not classic rachitic metaphyseal changes.
Osteopetrosis causes abnormally dense bones from osteoclast failure.
key_expl: Bowing, widened wrists, and poor growth in a child with vitamin D deficiency indicate rickets.
objective: Recognize nutritional rickets from impaired bone mineralization during growth.

sources.title: Rickets
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes rickets as defective mineralization in children commonly caused by vitamin D deficiency.

sources.title: Vitamin D
sources.support: NIH ODS describes vitamin D deficiency as causing rickets in children.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Immune-mediated vascular injury and fibroblast activation lead to excessive collagen deposition in skin and internal organs.
vignette: A 43-year-old woman has Raynaud phenomenon, progressive tightening of the skin of her fingers, reflux, and decreased oral aperture.
distractor_notes: SLE is characterized by multisystem autoimmunity but not progressive skin thickening and sclerodactyly.
Dermatomyositis causes proximal muscle weakness with characteristic rash.
Rheumatoid arthritis causes symmetric inflammatory arthritis rather than sclerodactyly.
Psoriasis causes scaly plaques and nail changes, not systemic fibrosis.
key_expl: Raynaud phenomenon plus sclerodactyly and esophageal dysfunction strongly indicate systemic sclerosis.
objective: Recognize systemic sclerosis from vascular, cutaneous, and gastrointestinal fibrosis.

sources.title: Scleroderma
sources.support: NIAMS describes systemic sclerosis as an autoimmune disease causing skin thickening and internal-organ fibrosis.

sources.title: Scleroderma
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes Raynaud phenomenon, skin tightening, and digestive involvement.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Immune-mediated inflammatory injury of skeletal muscle and skin causes symmetric proximal muscle weakness with characteristic heliotrope and Gottron lesions.
vignette: A 45-year-old woman has progressive difficulty rising from a chair and lifting objects overhead. Examination shows a violaceous periorbital rash and scaly papules over the knuckles.
distractor_notes: Polymyalgia rheumatica causes aching and stiffness in older adults without characteristic muscle inflammation or rash.
Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness without heliotrope or Gottron lesions.
Systemic sclerosis causes skin thickening and fibrosis rather than inflammatory proximal myopathy with this rash.
Duchenne muscular dystrophy presents in young boys.
key_expl: Proximal inflammatory myopathy with heliotrope rash and Gottron papules is classic dermatomyositis.
objective: Recognize dermatomyositis from proximal weakness and characteristic rash.

sources.title: Dermatomyositis
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes dermatomyositis as inflammatory muscle disease with proximal weakness and characteristic skin rash.

sources.title: Inflammatory Myopathies
sources.support: NINDS describes dermatomyositis as inflammatory muscle weakness with distinctive skin findings.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein disrupt keratinocyte adhesion within the epidermis, causing flaccid bullae and mucosal erosions.
vignette: A 52-year-old woman has painful oral erosions and fragile flaccid blisters on the trunk. Gentle pressure causes the epidermis to shear.
lead: Which adhesion structure is primarily targeted?
distractors: Hemidesmosomes attaching epidermis to basement membrane
Type IV collagen in basement membrane
distractor_notes: Hemidesmosomal targets are characteristic of bullous pemphigoid, which has tense bullae.
Type IV collagen disorders cause basement-membrane disease such as Alport syndrome.
Endothelial tight junction injury does not cause pemphigus.
Neutrophil integrin defects cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency.
key_expl: Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by anti-desmoglein antibodies that disrupt desmosomal adhesion.
objective: Link flaccid mucocutaneous bullae to desmosomal autoantibodies.
clues: flaccid bullae with positive Nikolsky sign

sources.title: Pemphigus
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes pemphigus as autoimmune blistering caused by loss of adhesion between skin cells.

sources.title: Pemphigus
sources.support: NIAMS describes autoantibodies disrupting proteins that hold epidermal cells together.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins at the dermal-epidermal junction cause subepidermal blister formation and tense bullae.
vignette: A 78-year-old man develops intensely pruritic, tense bullae on the trunk and flexural surfaces. Oral mucosa is spared.
lead: Which structure is most likely targeted?
distractor_notes: Desmosomal antibodies cause pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid bullae and mucosal disease.
Type I collagen defects produce connective-tissue fragility rather than autoimmune tense bullae.
Keratin 14 defects cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex from birth.
Melanocyte destruction causes vitiligo.
key_expl: Bullous pemphigoid is a subepidermal autoimmune blistering disease caused by hemidesmosomal autoantibodies.
objective: Differentiate bullous pemphigoid from pemphigus by blister level and target structure.
clues: elderly patient with tense pruritic bullae

sources.title: Bullous pemphigoid
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes bullous pemphigoid as an autoimmune blistering disorder producing tense bullae.

sources.title: Pemphigoid
sources.support: NIAMS describes pemphigoid as autoantibody-mediated separation at the basement membrane zone.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Malignant transformation of melanocytes produces an asymmetric evolving pigmented lesion with irregular borders and color variation.
vignette: A 49-year-old man has a pigmented lesion that has enlarged over 8 months. It is asymmetric, has irregular borders, and contains black, brown, and red areas.
distractor_notes: Seborrheic keratoses are usually well-circumscribed waxy stuck-on lesions.
Basal cell carcinomas are typically pearly papules with telangiectasias rather than evolving multicolored pigmented lesions.
Actinic keratoses are rough scaly premalignant lesions on sun-exposed skin.
Dermatofibromas are firm benign papules or nodules, often with a dimple sign.
key_expl: An evolving asymmetric lesion with irregular borders and variegated pigmentation is highly suspicious for melanoma.
objective: Recognize melanoma using classic ABCDE warning features.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals deposit in cartilage and synovium, triggering acute neutrophilic inflammation.
vignette: A 72-year-old man has abrupt knee pain and swelling. Synovial fluid shows rhomboid-shaped crystals with weak positive birefringence.
distractor_notes: Gout has needle-shaped negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals.
Septic arthritis does not produce birefringent crystals as the defining finding.
Rheumatoid arthritis is chronic symmetric inflammatory arthritis.
Osteoarthritis is degenerative and does not cause acute crystal-induced inflammation.
key_expl: Rhomboid positively birefringent crystals indicate calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease.
objective: Distinguish pseudogout from gout by crystal morphology.

sources.support: MedlinePlus describes pseudogout as calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis.

sources.support: NIAMS describes CPP crystal deposition as causing acute inflammatory arthritis.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Bacteremia can seed metaphyseal bone, where sluggish blood flow favors microbial deposition and inflammatory bone destruction.
vignette: A 9-year-old boy has fever and focal tibial pain. MRI shows metaphyseal marrow edema and blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus.
distractor_notes: Ewing sarcoma can cause bone pain and fever but would not be established by matching positive S aureus blood cultures.
Osteosarcoma is a malignant bone tumor, usually with destructive metaphyseal mass.
Septic bursitis affects superficial bursal tissue, not marrow.
JIA causes chronic inflammatory arthritis, not focal marrow infection with bacteremia.
key_expl: Fever, focal bone pain, MRI marrow changes, and S aureus bacteremia indicate hematogenous osteomyelitis.
objective: Recognize acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in a child.

sources.title: Osteomyelitis
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes osteomyelitis as bone infection often caused by bacteria including S aureus.

sources.title: Osteomyelitis

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Malignant osteoblasts produce osteoid, commonly arising in metaphyses of long bones in adolescents.
vignette: A 16-year-old boy has progressive pain and swelling around the distal femur. Imaging shows a destructive metaphyseal lesion with a sunburst periosteal reaction.
distractor_notes: Ewing sarcoma usually arises in the diaphysis and can show an onion-skin periosteal reaction.
Chondrosarcoma typically affects older adults and produces cartilaginous matrix.
Osteoid osteoma is a small benign painful lesion often relieved by NSAIDs.
Giant cell tumor usually occurs in the epiphysis after skeletal maturity.
key_expl: An adolescent with a metaphyseal destructive bone lesion and sunburst periosteal reaction has osteosarcoma.
objective: Recognize osteosarcoma from age, location, and radiographic pattern.

sources.title: Osteosarcoma and Undifferentiated Pleomorphic Sarcoma of Bone
sources.support: NCI describes osteosarcoma as a malignant bone tumor common in adolescents and often arising near the knee.

sources.title: Bone Cancer
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes osteosarcoma as a primary bone cancer often affecting children and young adults.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Fixed left ventricular outflow obstruction causes pressure overload, concentric hypertrophy, exertional syncope, angina, and heart failure.
vignette: A 76-year-old man has exertional chest pain and syncope. Examination reveals a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids.
distractor_notes: Mitral regurgitation causes a holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla.
Aortic regurgitation causes an early diastolic decrescendo murmur.
Mitral stenosis causes a diastolic rumble with opening snap.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can cause a systolic murmur but classically varies with preload and occurs in a different clinical context.
key_expl: Exertional syncope and angina with a carotid-radiating systolic ejection murmur indicate aortic stenosis.
objective: Diagnose aortic stenosis from classic symptoms and murmur.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Papillary muscle rupture after myocardial infarction causes abrupt loss of mitral leaflet support, severe regurgitation, and pulmonary edema.
vignette: Three days after an inferior myocardial infarction, a patient develops sudden pulmonary edema and a new loud holosystolic murmur at the apex.
lead: Which mechanical complication is most likely?
distractor_notes: Free-wall rupture causes hemopericardium and tamponade rather than an apical holosystolic murmur.
Septal rupture causes a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border.
Aortic dissection is unrelated to the timing and classic post-MI regurgitant murmur.
Tamponade produces hypotension and muffled heart sounds rather than acute MR.
key_expl: Papillary muscle rupture can occur several days after MI and causes acute severe mitral regurgitation with pulmonary edema.
objective: Identify papillary muscle rupture as a post-MI cause of acute mitral regurgitation.
clues: new apical holosystolic murmur with pulmonary edema

sources.title: Mitral regurgitation
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes mitral regurgitation as failure of the mitral valve to close effectively.

sources.title: Heart Attack Complications
sources.support: NHLBI describes structural complications after myocardial infarction.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Diastolic backflow from aorta to left ventricle causes volume overload, increased stroke volume, widened pulse pressure, and eccentric ventricular dilation.
vignette: A 45-year-old man has bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure. Auscultation reveals an early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border.
lead: Which ventricular adaptation is most expected in chronic disease?
correct: Eccentric left ventricular hypertrophy from volume overload
distractors: Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy from pure pressure overload
Left atrial hypertrophy without ventricular change
distractor_notes: Concentric hypertrophy is more typical of chronic pressure overload such as aortic stenosis.
The primary volume load is on the left ventricle, not right ventricle.
Chronic regurgitation produces substantial remodeling.
The left ventricle, not only the atrium, receives regurgitant volume each diastole.
key_expl: Chronic aortic regurgitation imposes a volume load on the left ventricle, producing eccentric hypertrophy and dilation.
objective: Predict eccentric hypertrophy in chronic aortic regurgitation.

sources.title: Aortic regurgitation
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes aortic regurgitation as backward flow into the left ventricle.

sources.title: Heart Valve Diseases
sources.support: NHLBI describes valve regurgitation as backward blood flow causing chamber volume stress.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Chaotic atrial electrical activity eliminates coordinated atrial contraction and produces an irregularly irregular ventricular response.
vignette: A 72-year-old woman has palpitations. Pulse is irregularly irregular. ECG shows no discrete P waves and variable R-R intervals.
distractor_notes: Atrial flutter typically shows organized sawtooth flutter waves.
Sinus arrhythmia retains P waves before each QRS.
Ventricular tachycardia is a wide-complex regular or near-regular tachyarrhythmia.
First-degree AV block has prolonged PR intervals but organized sinus rhythm.
key_expl: Absent P waves with an irregularly irregular rhythm is classic atrial fibrillation.

sources.title: Atrial fibrillation
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes atrial fibrillation as an irregular heart rhythm from disorganized atrial activity.

sources.title: Atrial Fibrillation
sources.support: NHLBI describes chaotic atrial signaling and irregular ventricular rhythm.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: An accessory atrioventricular pathway bypasses the AV node, causing ventricular pre-excitation with short PR interval and delta wave and enabling reentrant tachycardia.
vignette: A 23-year-old man has recurrent episodes of sudden palpitations. Baseline ECG shows a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke of the QRS complex.
lead: Which anatomic abnormality is most likely present?
distractors: Complete absence of the sinoatrial node
distractor_notes: SA node absence would impair normal rhythm generation, not cause pre-excitation.
AV nodal fibrosis causes conduction delay or block, not a short PR and delta wave.
An isolated ventricular pacemaker does not explain the characteristic baseline pre-excitation pattern.
PDA is a vascular congenital lesion unrelated to electrical pre-excitation.
key_expl: WPW is caused by an accessory AV pathway that bypasses the normal AV nodal delay.
objective: Connect short PR and delta wave with an accessory AV pathway.

sources.title: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes WPW as an accessory electrical pathway causing pre-excitation and tachycardia.

sources.title: Arrhythmia
sources.support: NHLBI describes abnormal conduction pathways as causes of arrhythmia.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Severe pump failure lowers cardiac output and arterial pressure while increasing ventricular filling pressures and systemic vascular resistance through compensatory vasoconstriction.
vignette: A patient with a large myocardial infarction is hypotensive, cool and clammy, with pulmonary edema and elevated jugular venous pressure.
lead: Which hemodynamic profile is most likely?
correct: Low cardiac output, high systemic vascular resistance, high pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
distractors: High cardiac output, low systemic vascular resistance, low wedge pressure
Low cardiac output, low systemic vascular resistance, low wedge pressure
High cardiac output, high systemic vascular resistance, high wedge pressure
Normal cardiac output, normal systemic vascular resistance, low wedge pressure
distractor_notes: High-output low-SVR physiology is more consistent with early distributive shock.
Low-output low-SVR low-filling-pressure physiology does not fit pump failure with congestion.
Cardiogenic shock does not typically have high cardiac output.
Normal hemodynamics do not fit severe shock.
key_expl: Pump failure causes low output and high filling pressure; reflex vasoconstriction raises SVR.

sources.title: Cardiogenic shock
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes cardiogenic shock as severe failure of the heart to pump enough blood.

sources.title: Cardiogenic Shock
sources.support: NHLBI describes reduced cardiac output and congestion in cardiogenic shock.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: An intimal tear permits blood to enter the aortic media and create a false lumen, producing abrupt tearing pain and pulse or pressure asymmetry.
vignette: A 61-year-old hypertensive man develops sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back. Blood pressure differs markedly between arms.
distractor_notes: Pericarditis causes positional pleuritic pain and diffuse ECG changes.
PE causes pleuritic dyspnea and thromboembolic risk factors, not classic tearing pain with pulse asymmetry.
Stable angina is exertional and transient.
Reflux does not cause sudden tearing pain with vascular asymmetry.
key_expl: Abrupt tearing pain radiating to the back with interarm blood-pressure difference is classic aortic dissection.
objective: Recognize aortic dissection from its characteristic pain and vascular findings.

sources.title: Aortic dissection
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes sudden severe chest or back pain and pulse differences in aortic dissection.

sources.title: Aortic Aneurysm
sources.support: NHLBI describes aortic wall tearing and life-threatening complications.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Rapid pericardial fluid accumulation raises intrapericardial pressure, restricts diastolic filling, equalizes chamber pressures, and lowers stroke volume.
vignette: After a penetrating chest injury, a patient is hypotensive with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds.
lead: Which physiologic abnormality most directly causes the hypotension?
correct: Impaired ventricular diastolic filling from elevated pericardial pressure
distractors: Excessive left ventricular afterload from aortic stenosis
Increased venous return to the right heart
Severe bradycardia from SA node failure
distractor_notes: Aortic stenosis is unrelated to the acute traumatic setting and Beck triad.
Loss of vascular tone causes distributive shock and does not produce distended neck veins plus muffled heart sounds.
Venous return is functionally impeded, not increased in a useful way.
Bradycardia is not the defining mechanism of tamponade shock.
key_expl: Tamponade compresses the heart and prevents normal diastolic filling, reducing stroke volume and blood pressure.
objective: Explain tamponade hypotension through impaired diastolic filling.

sources.title: Cardiac tamponade
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes tamponade as pericardial pressure that impairs heart filling and output.

sources.title: Pericardial Disease
sources.support: NHLBI describes fluid accumulation around the heart causing compression and impaired pumping.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Anterior malalignment of the infundibular septum causes right ventricular outflow obstruction, ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy.
vignette: A cyanotic infant has a harsh systolic murmur and episodes of worsening cyanosis relieved by squatting later in childhood. Imaging shows a VSD and overriding aorta.
lead: Which developmental abnormality best explains the defect complex?
correct: Anterior displacement of the infundibular septum
distractors: Failure of endocardial cushions to fuse
Persistence of the left fourth aortic arch only
Failure of atrial septum primum formation
distractor_notes: Endocardial cushion defects cause atrioventricular septal defects.
Neural tube closure failure causes CNS malformations.
Aortic arch persistence alone does not produce the TOF tetrad.
Atrial septation defects cause ASDs, not TOF.
key_expl: Tetralogy of Fallot results from malalignment of the conal/infundibular septum.
objective: Relate TOF anatomy to infundibular septal malalignment.
clues: cyanosis with VSD and overriding aorta

sources.title: Tetralogy of Fallot
sources.support: CDC describes the four structural abnormalities of tetralogy of Fallot.

sources.title: Tetralogy of Fallot
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes TOF as a congenital combination of VSD, pulmonary outflow obstruction, overriding aorta, and RV hypertrophy.
